plot: Second person: you live in the lead-mining village of Eyam in 1665-66; chapters cover your home, job and food, the cloth with fleas, plague symptoms, the choice of Mompesson and Stanley to quarantine the village, the rules (boundary stones, vinegar coins, church in Cucklett Delf), the August 1666 peak, Elizabeth Hancock, the last death on November 1, 1666, and the last chapter's open mystery of why some people never got sick.

beats.say: September 1665. A tailor in a tiny English village opened a bundle of cloth from London. A week later, he was dead. Within fourteen months, two hundred and sixty of his neighbors would be dead too.
Nobody leaves this village. Not one person. Not even if you have kin on the other side of that hill.
Not even my sister? She lives just three miles away!
This is Eyam, in the hills of Derbyshire, England, in the year 1666. You live here. And you are about to make the hardest choice of your life.
Would you stay inside a sealed village, knowing the plague is spreading, so that strangers you will never meet can live?
Let's go through your life, one question at a time. Your job, your food, your home, and the day everything changed.
And at the very end, a mystery that scientists still cannot answer.
Chapter one. Where do you live?
Eyam is a lead mining village high in the Peak District. Nobody is sure how many people lived here. Some say about three hundred and fifty. Others say seven hundred.
Even at seven hundred, that's about the size of one big American high school. Everybody knows your name, your family and your business.
Your home is a small stone cottage. The floor is packed dirt. The roof is heavy stone slabs, and in winter, the animals might sleep right next door.
You probably have one or two rooms, a fire, and a bed full of straw. Everyone in your family sleeps close together.
Chapter two. What is your job?
If you're a man, you most likely mine lead, working deep underground with just a candle. If you're a woman, you farm, spin wool and cook.
It is back-breaking work, and the pay is small. But lead pays better than a farm, and people in the hills are proud of it.
And on Sunday you come to my church. Whether you like me or not.
Chapter three. What do you eat?
Oatcakes and porridge. Barley bread. A little cheese, and some weak ale, since the water is not always safe to drink.
Meat is for special days. Most families keep a pig or a few sheep, and use every part of the animal.
My husband works the farm. My children help me. We are poor, but we are fed.
And what do you wear? Rough wool and linen, made by hand. You may own just two outfits, and you wear the same one for weeks.
Washing is rare, and soap costs money. That's another reason the fleas move in so easily.
Life is hard in 1665. But in Eyam, people know each other, and they look out for each other.
Chapter four. The cloth.
In late summer of 1665, a bundle of cloth arrives from London for the village tailor. A man named George Viccars opens it up.
The cloth is damp, so he hangs it by the fire to dry. What he doesn't know is that tiny fleas are hiding inside. And the fleas carry the plague.
On September seventh, Viccars is dead. That's the first death. Soon, the others in his house are sick too.
Nobody in 1665 knows what fleas can do. People believe plague floats in bad air. So they burn herbs and carry flowers.
Quick question. How do you know you have the plague?
First, a fever and a terrible headache. Then painful lumps swell up under your arms or in your groin. Some grow as big as an egg.
Dark spots may appear on the skin. Most people died within about a week, and some in just a few days.
We rub herbs on the lumps. We burn sweet wood. We pray. What else can we do?
Doctors had no idea what caused it. Some told people to smoke tobacco, hang bundles of herbs on the door, or keep a bowl of vinegar by the bed.
None of it worked. The only real protection was to avoid the fleas, and nobody knew the fleas were the problem.
In London, the same plague kills about a hundred thousand people in just a few months. About one in five Londoners. You've only heard rumors.
Chapter five. The choice.
By winter, forty-two people in Eyam have died. Then the cold slows the fleas, and the deaths almost stop.
But spring comes. And the sickness comes back with it. Families start packing carts. They want to run for their lives.
Now two men step forward. The new rector, William Mompesson, and the old rector, Thomas Stanley. They did not even agree about religion.
Stanley had lost his job as rector years before, because he was a Puritan. But when the plague came, the village listened to him anyway.
He and Mompesson visited the sick, buried the dead, and held the village together. For many families, they were the only help they had.
If you run, you carry the sickness with you. To Bakewell. To Sheffield. To thousands who've done nothing wrong.
So we must stay. All of us. And I will stay with you. I will not leave this village.
They talked and talked, and in the early summer of 1666, Eyam agreed. The whole village locked itself in.
I don't want to die. But I don't want my sister to die either. All right. I'll stay.
Chapter six. The rules.
Rule one. Nobody goes out, and nobody comes in. A ring of stones marks the edge of the village.
So how do you eat? Neighbors leave food on a stone at the edge. You leave money in return, and you never touch each other.
And the money goes into holes or a well filled with vinegar. People then believed vinegar could clean away the sickness.
A rich neighbor, the Earl of Devonshire, even sends food and medicine from his big house, Chatsworth. It's the only reason you can eat.
And think about your wallet. The lead mines are quiet now, because you can't sell your lead outside the village. No market means no money.
So what do you do all day? You farm a little. You pray. You check on your neighbors from across the road, and you wait.
Rule two. No more church indoors. Families stand apart in a rocky hollow called Cucklett Delf, and Mompesson preaches to them from a natural stone arch.
Rule three. No burials in the churchyard. Each family has to bury its own dead, usually in a field or garden, as fast as they can.
And one more thing. Once a house had the plague, the fleas jumped from bed to bed. Whole families got sick together.
That's why neighbors were so afraid. When a family fell sick, they usually shut the door and left it alone.
It's frightening. But for the first weeks, it seems to work. And then comes August.
Every few days, Mompesson writes a letter asking for food and medicine. The answers come, and each time, the helpers wait far outside the stones.
They can't come in. But they can leave bread on a rock. And that is enough to keep us alive.
Chapter seven. The worst month.
The summer is very hot. Hot weather makes fleas more active, and the plague runs wild. At its worst, five or six people die every day.
And this is the saddest part. A farm woman named Elizabeth Hancock lost her husband and six children in just eight days.
No one can help me. If they touch them, they will die too. So I must do it myself.
She dragged each body to a field near their farm, and she buried them with her own hands. The graves are still there. They're called the Riley Graves.
It's said that people from a nearby village stood on a hill and watched her. They wanted to help, but they were too afraid to get close.
Chapter eight. A love story.
Tradition tells of a girl named Emmott Sydall. Her sweetheart, Rowland Torre, lived in a village outside the stones.
They met in the rocky hollow, and called out to each other across the gap. They could see each other but not touch.
Then Emmott caught the plague. Six of the eight people in her family died that year.
Chapter nine. The rector.
Mompesson had told you he would stay, and he did. He prayed over the sick, and wrote letters begging for help.
His wife, Catherine, helped him nurse the sick. On a warm evening in late August, she mentioned a sweet smell in the air.
It was a known sign of plague. A day or so later, Catherine Mompesson was dead. She was twenty-seven years old.
He buried her himself in the churchyard. He expected to die next. But he didn't.
Chapter ten. How does it end?
In September, the deaths slow down. In October, almost nobody gets sick. The village waits, and waits, afraid to believe it.
Then, on November first, 1666, a farm worker named Abraham Morten dies. He turns out to be the very last.
In fourteen months, about two hundred and sixty people died, in nearly eighty families. But the plague never spread to the towns around them.
To get a feel for it, two hundred and sixty people is more than four full school buses. Gone from one small hilltop village.
Think about how brave that was. Nobody forced them. Nobody had a doctor, a vaccine, or a drug. They only had a promise to each other.
So did the village's choice work? In 2016, scientists ran the numbers again, with computer models. They asked a hard question.
Did locking Eyam in save thousands of lives outside? Or did it just trap the people inside with the fleas? Experts still argue about it.
It took more than two hundred years to learn the truth. In the 1890s, scientists finally found the germ, and proved that fleas from rats were spreading it.
So Mompesson was wrong about bad air, and wrong about vinegar. But he was right about one big thing. Keeping sick people away from healthy people saves lives.
Chapter eleven. The mystery.
Not everyone in Eyam got sick. Some people lived in the same house as the dying, and never caught it at all.
Mompesson himself lived. And so did a gravedigger named Marshall Howe, who had the plague early, got better, and buried dozens of his neighbors.
Why did they live? Back then, people said it was God's will. But for hundreds of years, nobody had a better answer.
In the 1990s, some scientists wondered if certain Eyam families carried a gene that protected them. The idea became famous.
But later studies cast doubt on it. So today, nobody can say for sure why some people in Eyam survived.
If you go there, you can still find the boundary stone with holes drilled in the top, where villagers once dropped their coins in vinegar.
Mompesson lived another forty years. He moved away in 1669 and became the minister of a village in Nottinghamshire, and he died in 1709.
And Eyam never forgot. Every year, on the last Sunday in August, people still gather in the rocky hollow to remember what the village did.
Walk the lanes of Eyam today, and you'll see small green plaques on the old stone cottages. Each one lists the names of the family who died inside.
So would you have stayed? Would you have let the stones close around you, to save people you would never meet?
Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more true history.

long.title: Locked In With the Plague: Eyam, 1666 🕯️
long.description:
Would you have stayed? Tell me in the comments.

In 1665 a bundle of cloth from London brought the plague to a small English hill village. Then the villagers made a choice almost nobody else would make: they sealed themselves in, so the sickness would not reach the towns around them. Your food, your home, the rules, the worst month, and a mystery that scientists still cannot fully answer.
